title: Hash Set: Longest Consecutive Sequence
oneLiner: The longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n): put everything in a set and only start counting from numbers that begin a run.
keyTakeaway: Sorting gives O(n log n). For O(n), put the numbers in a hash set and walk upwards only from x where x - 1 is NOT in the set, the start of a run. Each run is then walked once from its start, so the inner while loop does n steps in total across the whole pass, not per number.
explanation:
Given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive values (x, x + 1, x + 2, ...) that all appear in it. Their positions don't matter. [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] gives 4, for 1, 2, 3, 4. Duplicates count once. The target is O(n) time.

Sorting and scanning for runs works in O(n log n) and is worth saying first. To beat it, use a hash set for O(1) "is this value present?" checks. The naive set version, "for each x, count upwards while x + 1 is in the set", is O(n²) on input like [1, 2, 3, ..., n], because every number re-walks the rest of the run.

The fix is one condition: only start counting from x if x - 1 is not in the set. Then x is the smallest number of its run, and every run is walked exactly once, from its start. A number in the middle of a run is skipped in O(1). The inner while loop therefore takes n steps in total over the whole outer loop, which is why the nested loops are still O(n). Iterate over the set rather than the array, so duplicates don't start the same run twice.

O(n) time on average (hash set operations), O(n) space for the set. Union-Find, joining x with x + 1, also works and is a good follow-up answer.

The visualization runs [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]: the left side is the array, the right side shows each run start and its length.

recognitionSignals: "Consecutive" values in an unsorted array with an O(n) requirement.
A nested loop that would be O(n²) unless each element is only ever the start of one walk.
gotchas: Counting upwards from every number is O(n²); only start where x - 1 is missing.
Looping over the array instead of the set makes duplicate run starts walk twice.
An empty array has answer 0, not 1.
confusableWith: Longest Increasing Subsequence keeps the array order and allows gaps; this ignores positions and needs values with no gaps.
Two Sum also uses a hash set for O(1) lookups, but looks for one partner per element, not a chain.

complexity.note: Building the set is O(n). Each number is skipped in O(1) or starts the one walk of its run, so the inner loop takes n steps in total across all runs. The set holds up to n values.

referenceSolutions.python:
def longest_consecutive(nums):
    values = set(nums)
    best = 0
    for x in values:
        if x - 1 in values:  # not the start of a run
            continue
        y = x
        while y + 1 in values:  # each run is walked once, from its start
            y += 1
        best = max(best, y - x + 1)
    return best
